Scale-free coefficients of a fitted directed layer

Source: R/dag_layer.R
mc_dag_coefficients.Rd

Reports, with standard errors and intervals, the quantities of the directed layer that do not depend on the scale on which the residual dependence is measured. Under a diagonal rescaling \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_b\mapsto\mathbf A\boldsymbol\Sigma_b\mathbf A\) the raw coefficients move as \(\gamma_{jk}\mapsto\gamma_{jk}a_j/a_k\) and the innovation variances as \(\delta_j\mapsto a_j^2\delta_j\), whereas $$\gamma^*_{jk}=\gamma_{jk}\left(\frac{\Sigma_{b,kk}}{\Sigma_{b,jj}} \right)^{1/2},\qquad R^2_{j\cdot P_j}=1-\frac{\delta_j}{\Sigma_{b,jj}}$$ are invariant. These are the quantities to report: they play for the directed layer the role that partial correlations play for the undirected one.

Usage

mc_dag_coefficients(
  fit,
  variability = c("model", "empirical", "two_stage"),
  level = 0.95,
  interval = c("delta", "fixed_factor"),
  cluster = NULL,
  small_sample = FALSE,
  r2_interval = c("wald", "logit"),
  method = c("auto", "shortcut", "full")
)

# S3 method for class 'mcg_dag_coef'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

fit

an object of class "mcglm_graph" fitted with the DAG layer.

variability

"model" for \(\mathbf J_n^{-1}\), "empirical" for the sandwich, or "two_stage" for the sandwich corrected for the estimation of the residuals.

level

confidence level of the intervals.

interval

"delta" (default) or "fixed_factor", the interval for \(\gamma^*\) as described above.

cluster, small_sample

passed to mc_vcov_graph for the empirical forms.

r2_interval

"wald" (default), symmetric on the scale of \(R^2\), or "logit", symmetric on the scale of \(\log\{R^2/(1-R^2)\}\) and mapped back, so that the bounds stay inside \((0, 1)\). A response without parents has \(R^2=0\) by construction, and its interval is that point.

method

for variability = "two_stage", the route of the correction, "auto" (default), "shortcut" or "full", as in mc_vcov_graph. It has no meaning for the other two forms and is refused with them when it is not "auto".

x

an object of class "mcg_dag_coef".

...

ignored.

Value

An object of class "mcg_dag_coef": a list with edges, one row per directed edge with the raw and standardized coefficient, the standard error of each, the Wald statistic of the raw coefficient, its p-value and the two intervals, and nodes, one row per response with the innovation variance and its standard error, and \(R^2_{j\cdot P_j}\) with its standard error and interval. The gradients of \(\gamma^*\) and of \(R^2\) travel in the attributes "gradient_std" and "gradient_r2". The list also records variability, level, interval, r2_interval and two_stage_method, the route taken with variability = "two_stage" and NA otherwise. The print method shows the main columns and returns x invisibly.

What the coefficients are

\(\gamma_{jk}\) is the coefficient of response \(k\) in the linear projection of the residual component of response \(j\) on those of its parents, under the ordering of the fit, and \(\delta_j\) is the variance left by that projection. The factorization does not by itself define a causal model. Reading a coefficient as the effect of an intervention requires a linear structural model with independent exogenous innovations, the correct ordering, no unobserved confounding and equations that are invariant under intervention. The fit checks none of these.

When the first stage is such a rescaling

The first stage acts on the residual covariance, to first order, as a diagonal rescaling under conditions (b) and (c) of the section "What the correction reaches" of mc_vcov_graph: a correctly specified mean, and a conditional residual covariance that does not depend on the covariates. Under them the direction in which the first stage moves \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_b\) is \(\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Sigma_b+ \boldsymbol\Sigma_b\boldsymbol\Lambda\) with \(\boldsymbol\Lambda\) diagonal, whatever the parametrization, and the quantities above do not see it. The two conditions are sufficient: with the constant variance function (c) is not needed, and with a variance function that depends on the mean a residual correlation that changes with the covariates moves \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_b\) in a direction the standardized coefficients do see. The finer characterization of the section "When the shortcut is right" of mc_vcov_graph was established for the undirected layer; for this one the sufficient conditions are the ones to rely on. The package checks none of them.

What the standard errors cover

They come from mc_vcov_graph and refer to the second stage conditionally on the estimated residuals, unless variability = "two_stage". The empirical forms use the observed Hessian of the working criterion; the model form uses the Pearson sensitivity and requires correct second-moment specification and its Gaussian working variability identity. The Wald statistic of \(\gamma_{jk}=0\) is invariant under the diagonal rescaling, because the coefficient and its standard error are both multiplied by \(a_j/a_k\), so under (b) and (c) the test is adequate to first order where the raw coefficient is not.

Intervals for the scale-free quantities

Both \(\gamma^*_{jk}\) and \(R^2_{j\cdot P_j}\) are functions of \((\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\delta)\), through the coefficient itself and through \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_b=\mathbf T^{-1}\mathbf D\mathbf T^{-\top}\), so their variance follows by the delta method with the analytical gradients $$\frac{\partial\gamma^*_{jk}}{\partial\theta_d}= \frac{\partial\gamma_{jk}}{\partial\theta_d}\,f_{jk}+ \frac{\gamma^*_{jk}}{2}\left(\frac{\dot\Sigma_{b,d,kk}}{\Sigma_{b,kk}}- \frac{\dot\Sigma_{b,d,jj}}{\Sigma_{b,jj}}\right),\qquad \frac{\partial R^2_{j\cdot P_j}}{\partial\theta_d}= -\frac{1}{\Sigma_{b,jj}}\frac{\partial\delta_j}{\partial\theta_d}+ \frac{\delta_j\,\dot\Sigma_{b,d,jj}}{\Sigma_{b,jj}^2},$$ with \(f_{jk}=(\Sigma_{b,kk}/\Sigma_{b,jj})^{1/2}\) and \(\dot{\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{b,d}=\partial\boldsymbol\Sigma_b/ \partial\theta_d\). That is interval = "delta", the default. With interval = "fixed_factor" the interval for \(\gamma^*\) is the one for \(\gamma\) multiplied by \(f_{jk}\) as if the factor were known, which leaves out the uncertainty of the variances in it. The interval for \(R^2\) is always by the delta method, since it has no fixed-factor analogue.

Examples

# \donttest{
set.seed(4); n <- 400; x <- rnorm(n)
y1 <- rnorm(n); y2 <- 0.6 * y1 + rnorm(n); y3 <- 0.4 * y2 + rnorm(n)
d <- data.frame(y1 = y1, y2 = y2, y3 = y3, x = x)
f <- mcglm_graph(list(y1 ~ x, y2 ~ x, y3 ~ x),
                 between_graph = mc_between_graph("dag"), data = d)
#> Automatic initial values selected.
mc_dag_coefficients(f)
#> Directed layer (model variability, level 0.95)
#> 
#> Edges (parent -> child):
#>   parent child    gamma gamma_std      se  se_std statistic   p_value
#> 1     y1    y2 0.538120  0.538120 0.04214 0.03552   12.7688 2.450e-37
#> 2     y1    y3 0.005664  0.005664 0.05431 0.05430    0.1043 9.169e-01
#> 3     y2    y3 0.399375  0.399375 0.05431 0.05114    7.3543 1.919e-13
#> 
#> Nodes:
#>   response n_parents  delta se_delta r_squared se_r_squared
#> 1       y1         0 0.9950  0.07036    0.0000      0.00000
#> 2       y2         1 0.7069  0.04998    0.2896      0.03823
#> 3       y3         2 0.8338  0.05896    0.1620      0.03373
# }
